topic: The baker/baker paradox — why occupations are remembered better than proper names

fact_check.claim: Semantically meaningful labels (an occupation) are recalled better than arbitrary proper names because they connect to existing associative networks — the 'baker/baker paradox' discussed alongside levels-of-processing research.
fact_check.source_hint: Craik & Lockhart's levels-of-processing framework; cognitive psychology literature on proper-name recall and the baker-baker paradox. Present as a well-known demonstration, not a single definitive study.

hooks: I'm a baker. I'm Baker. One sticks. One vanishes.
You'll forget my name in ten seconds. Not my job.
Your brain stores meaning, not labels.
titles: Why You Forget A Name In 10 Seconds (Baker/Baker Paradox)
'Baker' The Job Sticks. 'Baker' The Name Doesn't. Here's Why.
The Memory Trick That Fixes Forgetting Names

beats.vo: I'm a baker. I'm Baker. One sticks. One vanishes.
beats.visual: Two identical words side by side on frame 1; one starts fading immediately

beats.vo: Say both out loud. Ten seconds from now you'll remember the job, not the name.
beats.visual: Ten-second timer starts; presenter points at the camera

beats.vo: That's the baker-baker paradox. Same sound, same letters, completely different memory strength.
beats.visual: The two words get a strength bar each; one bar collapses

beats.vo: A job comes with a whole network: flour, ovens, early mornings, smell of bread.
beats.visual: Fast four-shot montage, each word appearing with its image

beats.vo: A name comes with nothing. It's an arbitrary label taped to a face.
beats.visual: A blank label slapping onto a silhouette; music drops

beats.vo: Your brain stores meaning, not labels. The moment you link a name to something — 'Baker, always wears red' — recall jumps. Repetition alone barely moves it.
beats.visual: Animated connection lines from a face to red jacket, then to the word Baker

beats.vo: So next time you forget a name, don't blame memory. Blame the missing connection.
beats.visual: Back to the two words from frame 1, now one connected by lines
Exact frame-1 composition restored for the loop

payoff: Names are arbitrary labels; memory needs a meaningful connection to hold onto.
cta: Which did you remember: the job or the name?
pinned_comment: Be honest: did you remember the JOB or the NAME? One word 👇 I'm collecting results for a follow-up.
description:
I'm a baker. I'm Baker. One sticks, one vanishes.

The baker-baker paradox: an occupation arrives with a whole network of meaning (flour, ovens, 4am), while a proper name is an arbitrary label with nothing to attach to. Link the name to a detail and recall jumps; repeating it barely helps.

Which did you remember: the job or the name?

Concept: levels of processing / proper-name recall. Educational summary.
